definition: A winemaking term for the part of the process when the grapes are left to “sit” on their skins after pressing, leaving time for (red) wines o gain their color from the pigment and anthocyanins in the skins.

A viticulture term for the use of mechanized methods to remove the grapes from the vines during harvest. Often looked at as industrialization, mechanized harvesting does not automatically mean lower quality, although many high-end wines use hand harvesting methods.
A viticulture term for the immediate area surrounding a wine region, and the climate that is most prevalent.

Madeira is a fortified wine from the Portuguese island of Madeira, located in the Atlantic Ocean southwest of mainland Portugal. Its defining feature is deliberate exposure to heat and oxygen during aging, a process that gives the wine unusual stability and allows many examples to age for decades or longer.
definition2: The principal noble varieties are Sercial, Verdelho, Bual, and Malvasia, traditionally associated with styles ranging from dry to richly sweet, while Tinta Negra is also widely used. Madeira commonly shows citrus peel, dried fruit, caramel, nuts, spice, and saline complexity, with acidity providing balance across its full range of sweetness.

definition: A wine tasting term that describes a “cooked” or “caramelized” aroma and flavor to a wine. This refers to the estufa process that some Madeira’s go through, rendering the wine with these unique characteristics.
A larger format style bottle which holds 1.5 liters of wine, or the equivalent of 2 bottles.

Malbec is a deeply colored red grape of French origin, historically associated with Cahors, but now most closely identified with Argentina, especially Mendoza. It typically produces full-bodied wines with blackberry and plum fruit, violet aromas, moderate to firm tannins, and notes of spice, cocoa, or tobacco, with high-altitude examples often showing greater freshness and aromatic lift.
A type of acid found in all fruit. Malic acid is high in green apples, giving off an abrasive texture and finish if levels are too high. See Malolactic fermentation below.

A winemaking term that describes the conversion of sharp malic acid (found in green apples) into lactic acid (found in milk). All red wines go through this process, with the most noticeable white wine seeing this treatment being Chardonnay, deriving its creamy and buttery texture front his process.
A strong, mass-market beer style made with adjuncts and higher alcohol content, often sold in large bottles or cans and associated with sweeter, fuller flavors.

A style of sherry, closely related to Fino, made in the seaside town of Sanlucar de Barrameda. This wine has more salinity than its Fino counterpart due to the proximity to the ocean and the violent breezes off the water that this region is famous for.

Marc, or eau-de-vie de marc, is a French pomace brandy distilled from the grape skins, seeds, and other solids left after winemaking, making it France’s counterpart to Italian grappa. Styles vary by region, with examples such as Marc de Bourgogne and Marc de Champagne ranging from fiery and rustic to smooth, aromatic, and barrel-aged.

Marche is a central Italian wine region stretching from the Apennine Mountains to the Adriatic Sea, with rolling hills and coastal influences supporting both fresh whites and structured reds. It is best known for Verdicchio from Castelli di Jesi and Matelica, alongside Montepulciano- and Sangiovese-based reds such as Rosso Conero and Rosso Piceno, plus local specialties including Pecorino and Lacrima di Morro d’Alba.

Margaret River is a premier wine region in Western Australia, located along a remote coastal area south of Perth. Despite producing only a small percentage of Australia’s total wine, it is considered one of the country’s most prestigious regions due to its consistently high quality. The climate is strongly influenced by the surrounding oceans, creating conditions similar to Bordeaux, which makes it ideal for Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay. The wines are known for their balance, structure, and elegance, often combining power with refined acidity. Margaret River also benefits from a relatively young industry, allowing producers to adopt modern techniques while focusing on quality from the start. Today, it stands as one of Australia’s benchmark regions for premium wine.

Marlborough is New Zealand’s largest and most famous wine region, located at the northeastern tip of the South Island and shaped by abundant sunshine, cool nights, low rainfall, and strong maritime influence. It is the global benchmark for Sauvignon Blanc, producing intensely aromatic wines with passion fruit, citrus, gooseberry, fresh herbs, and bright acidity, while Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, and sparkling wine also perform well across the Wairau, Awatere, and Southern Valleys.
Marsala is a fortified wine from western Sicily, traditionally made from grapes such as Grillo, Catarratto, and Inzolia, with styles ranging from dry to sweet and colors from golden to amber or ruby.

Marselan is a red grape created in France by crossing Cabernet Sauvignon with Grenache, combining deep color and structure with good heat tolerance and adaptability. It typically produces aromatic, medium- to full-bodied wines with dark berry and plum flavors, supple tannins, and increasing importance in warm regions such as southern France and China.

McLaren Vale is a prominent wine region in South Australia, located just south of Adelaide, known for its Mediterranean climate and diverse terroir. The region is especially famous for Shiraz, which often shows ripe fruit, richness, and a distinct savory, earthy character. Proximity to the ocean helps moderate temperatures, allowing for balanced wines with both power and freshness. McLaren Vale is also recognized for its innovation, including a strong focus on organic and biodynamic viticulture. Today, it stands as one of Australia’s most dynamic regions, producing a wide range of expressive red and white wines.
An alcoholic beverage made from fermented honey, sometimes blended with fruit or spices, representing one of the oldest known alcoholic drinks in the world.

Médoc is a major wine district of Bordeaux, located on the Left Bank between the Gironde estuary and the Atlantic Ocean. Its gravelly soils, maritime influence, and drainage capacity favor Cabernet Sauvignon, making structure a defining feature of the region’s most important red wines.
definition2: The district includes the broader Médoc and Haut-Médoc appellations, along with famous communal appellations such as Saint-Estèphe, Pauillac, Saint-Julien, and Margaux. Médoc wines are typically Cabernet-led blends with Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, and other permitted grapes, valued for tannin, cassis, cedar, graphite, longevity, and historic classification prestige.

definition: Melon de Bourgogne is a white grape variety best known as the sole grape used in Muscadet wines from the Loire Valley’s Pays Nantais, producing light-bodied, crisp wines with notes of lemon, green apple, and saline minerality. Often aged sur lie (on the lees) to add texture and complexity, Melon de Bourgogne excels with oysters and seafood, showcasing its bracing acidity and subtle, ocean-influenced character.

Mendocino County is a northern California wine region located above Sonoma County, with vineyards shaped by Pacific influence, inland valleys, mountain terrain, and significant organic and sustainable farming traditions. Its geography ranges from the cool Anderson Valley near the coast to warmer interior areas such as Redwood Valley, Ukiah Valley, and Potter Valley.
definition2: The county is best known for Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, sparkling wine, Zinfandel, Cabernet Sauvignon, Petite Sirah, and aromatic white varieties, depending on site and climate. Mendocino’s importance lies in its contrast between coastal freshness and inland ripeness, giving the region a broad identity that is less commercially dominant than Napa or Sonoma but highly distinctive within California wine.

definition: Mendoza is Argentina’s leading wine region, where high-altitude vineyards, intense sunlight, dry conditions, and cool Andean nights help grapes retain freshness while developing deep flavor. Best known for Malbec, the region also produces excellent Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, and increasingly distinctive wines that express its varied elevations, soils, and subregions.

Merlot is a red grape variety of Bordeaux origin, valued for its supple texture, moderate tannin, and ability to produce both accessible wines and age-worthy blends. It is one of the principal grapes of Bordeaux’s Right Bank, especially in Saint-Émilion and Pomerol, where clay soils often support wines of depth, flesh, and structural balance.
definition2: The grape is widely planted internationally and commonly shows plum, black cherry, red currant, cocoa, cedar, herbs, and earthy notes depending on climate and ripeness. Merlot is important both as a varietal wine and as a blending partner with Cabernet Sauvignon, where it can add softness, mid-palate volume, and generosity.

definition: The Meseta Central is Spain’s vast, high-elevation interior plateau, where intense sunlight, low rainfall, hot days, and cold nights create large temperature swings that help grapes ripen while retaining acidity. Its principal wine areas include Castilla y León in the north, home to Ribera del Duero, Rueda, Toro, and Cigales, and Castilla-La Mancha in the south, including La Mancha, Valdepeñas, Manchuela, and Almansa.
A viticulture term describing the immediate climactic conditions surrounding a vineyard, referring to its impact on the viticulture of that area.

The traditional method for making Champagne, in which the second fermentation occurs within the bottle. A legally protected term - only Champagne may wear this on the label - although the method is used the world over.
Winemakers outside Champagne using the Methode Champenoise may use this to describe the process on the label. They are legally prevented from using the term Methode Champenoise.
Large-format bottle that contains 6 liters of volume (8 bottles).

Mexico is a major beverage-producing nation best known for tequila and mezcal, geographically protected agave spirits rooted in regional raw materials, traditional methods, and distinct local cultures. Its wine industry dates to the early colonial period and now spans Baja California, Coahuila, Querétaro, Guanajuato, and other states.

Mezcal is a traditional Mexican spirit made from the agave plant, typically produced in Oaxaca, though several states have official denomination of origin. Unlike tequila—which must be made from only Blue Weber agave—mezcal can be made from dozens of agave varieties, including Espadín, Tobalá, and Tepeztate, each imparting its own unique flavor. Mezcal is most famously known for its distinct smoky character, which comes from roasting the agave hearts (piñas) in underground earthen ovens lined with hot stones and covered with plant matter and soil. Artisanal and ancestral production methods are often employed, involving natural fermentation, wood-fired copper or clay stills, and small-scale, family-owned palenques (distilleries).
A French winemaking term denoting residual sugar in the wine, and the drinker can definitely expect sweetness from these wines.

Montepulciano is a dark-skinned red grape grown mainly in central and southern Italy, especially Abruzzo, where it forms the basis of Montepulciano d’Abruzzo. It typically produces deeply colored, medium- to full-bodied wines with black cherry, plum, herbs, moderate acidity, and soft to firm tannins, and it should not be confused with Vino Nobile di Montepulciano, a Tuscan wine made primarily from Sangiovese.

Monterey County is a major wine region on California’s Central Coast, shaped by the cooling influence of Monterey Bay, the Salinas Valley, and the surrounding mountain ranges. Its vineyards extend from cold, wind-exposed northern sites to warmer southern zones, creating a long growing season where maritime influence preserves acidity while allowing gradual flavor development.
definition2: The county is especially important for Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Syrah, Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc, and Cabernet Sauvignon, depending on site and temperature. Key appellations include Santa Lucia Highlands, Arroyo Seco, Carmel Valley, Chalone, and the broader Monterey AVA, with the region’s identity rooted in climatic contrast and the movement of cool Pacific air through inland valleys.

definition: The Monticello AVA is a historic Virginia wine region surrounding Charlottesville in the central Piedmont, along the eastern slopes of the Blue Ridge Mountains and near Thomas Jefferson’s Monticello estate. Its rolling terrain, clay and granite-derived soils, and long growing season support grapes such as Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Viognier, Chardonnay, and Petit Manseng.
Morellino di Scansano is a red DOCG wine from southern Tuscany’s coastal Maremma, centered around the town of Scansano and made primarily from Sangiovese, locally called Morellino.
definition2: The warmer maritime climate typically produces ripe, approachable wines with cherry, plum, herbs, moderate tannins, and softer structure than many inland Tuscan Sangiovese wines.

definition: Morocco is a North African wine-producing country with a viticultural history shaped by Roman settlement, French colonial influence, and modern investment in quality-oriented vineyards. Most production is concentrated near the Atlantic-influenced zones around Meknès, Rabat, Casablanca, and the foothills of the Atlas Mountains, where elevation and ocean breezes help moderate heat.
definition2: The country is best known for red and rosé wines from varieties such as Syrah, Grenache, Carignan, Cinsault, Cabernet Sauvignon, and Mourvèdre, with smaller amounts of white wine also produced. Moroccan wine is significant because it shows how Mediterranean grape culture extends beyond southern Europe into North Africa, adapting French varieties and regional traditions to a warmer, drier climate.

definition: Mosel is one of Germany’s most important wine regions, following the Mosel River and its tributaries through a narrow, steep-sided valley near the borders of Luxembourg and France. Its vineyards are defined by dramatic slopes, slate soils, cool northern latitude, and river moderation, creating conditions where Riesling can ripen slowly while retaining high acidity.
definition2: The region is known for wines of delicacy, precision, low to moderate alcohol, and pronounced aromatic detail, often showing citrus, green apple, peach, florals, herbs, and mineral character. Mosel Riesling ranges from dry to intensely sweet, with the best examples valued for balance, transparency, and exceptional longevity.

definition: Mourvèdre is a thick-skinned, late-ripening red grape known for producing deeply colored, full-bodied wines with flavors of dark berries, earth, game, and spice, often supported by firm tannins and high alcohol. Thriving in warm, sun-soaked regions like Provence, Spain (as Monastrell), and parts of California, Mourvèdre is frequently used in GSM blends (Grenache–Syrah–Mourvèdre) to add structure, depth, and age-worthiness.
A warm, spiced red wine often served during colder months, typically infused with cinnamon, cloves, citrus, and sweeteners—popular in European holiday markets.

Müller-Thurgau is an early-ripening white grape created in Germany in 1882 by Hermann Müller, now understood to be a crossing of Riesling and Madeleine Royale. It typically produces light, soft, aromatic wines with apple, pear, peach, floral, and subtle muscat-like notes, but generally has lower acidity and less aging potential than Riesling.

Muscat is an ancient, highly aromatic family of white and dark-skinned grapes, known by names such as Moscato and Moscatel, with Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains among its most prized members. It produces wines ranging from dry and sparkling to richly sweet and fortified, typically showing orange blossom, grape, peach, apricot, citrus, and spice.

Muscat of Alexandria is an ancient, late-ripening member of the Muscat family, traditionally grown in warm Mediterranean climates for wine, raisins, and table grapes. Known as Zibibbo in Sicily and Muscat Gordo Blanco in Australia, it produces intensely aromatic wines with orange blossom, ripe peach, citrus, grape, and spice, ranging from dry to richly sweet and fortified.
The mixture of grape juice, stems, pips and skins that remains in the fermentation vat after pressing and before the fermentation kick starts.
A winemaking term that describes the addition of grape spirit to the fermentation vat in order to arrest the fermentation, leaving residual sugar in the wine. Also known as fortification.
